dbms-nosql:0.prompt: A social app needs queries like 'friends of my friends who also follow topic X', several hops deep, with low latency. Which database family fits most naturally?
options: Key-value store
Time-series database
Graph database
Wide-column store
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Graph databases store relationships as first-class edges, so each hop costs roughly in proportion to the neighbours visited, not the table size. Key-value and wide-column stores would need many round trips or heavy denormalization for multi-hop traversals.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: An IoT platform stores millions of sensor readings per minute, queries by time range, downsamples old data to hourly averages, and drops raw data after 30 days. Which database family is the most natural fit?
options: Time-series database
Graph database
Document database
Key-value cache
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Time-series databases are built for append-heavy timestamped data, with time-partitioned storage, compression, downsampling and retention policies. A document store can hold the data, but you'd build those features yourself.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: An auth service needs to look up session data by session id on every request, with automatic expiry after 30 minutes. Which store fits best?
options: Graph database
Key-value store with TTL support, such as Redis
Columnar analytics warehouse
Wide-column store with secondary indexes
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: This is a single-key lookup with expiry, which is exactly what in-memory key-value stores with TTL do well. A warehouse is built for scans, not millisecond point reads.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: An e-commerce catalog has products whose attributes vary widely by category (laptops have CPU and RAM, shirts have size and fabric) and are read as a whole. Which model fits most naturally?
options: Graph database with one node per attribute
Key-value store with one key per attribute
Time-series database
Document database storing each product as one document
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Documents hold nested, varying attributes per record and return the whole product in one read. One key per attribute turns each product page into many lookups and loses atomic updates of a product.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: Cassandra and similar wide-column stores use LSM trees (commit log, memtable, SSTables, compaction). What is the main trade-off of this design?
options: Writes are slow because every write updates a B-tree in place
Writes are cheap sequential appends, but reads may have to check several SSTables, and compaction uses background I/O
Reads are always one disk seek, but writes need a global lock
Data can't be deleted
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: LSM trees buffer writes in memory and flush immutable sorted files, which makes writes fast. Reads may merge several files (bloom filters help), and compaction rewrites data in the background. In-place B-tree updates are the opposite design.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: Why does a graph database usually beat a relational database on a 6-hop traversal over a large social graph?
options: Graph databases keep all data in RAM
Relational databases can't express recursive queries
Graph databases avoid disk I/O by compressing edges
Each hop follows stored adjacency directly, instead of an index-backed join whose cost grows with table size
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Graph engines traverse from a node to its neighbours through stored adjacency, so cost tracks the visited subgraph. In SQL each hop is another join (or a recursive CTE iteration) through indexes on large tables. SQL can express it (WITH RECURSIVE), so the second option is wrong.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: Which feature most clearly sets a purpose-built time-series database apart from a general-purpose document store?
options: Support for JSON values
Built-in retention policies, downsampling and time-chunked columnar compression
Secondary indexes
Horizontal sharding
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Automatic retention, continuous aggregates or downsampling, and compression tuned for timestamped series are the defining features. JSON, secondary indexes and sharding exist in many general-purpose stores.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: Which workloads are a good fit for a key-value store? Select all that apply.
options: Caching rendered pages by URL
Per-user rate-limit counters
A shopping cart looked up by user id
Ad-hoc reports joining orders, customers and products
Finding all users in a given city with no secondary index
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Key-value stores excel when every access is by a known key. Ad-hoc joins and lookups by non-key attributes need query flexibility or indexes that a pure key-value store doesn't provide.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: Which statements about wide-column stores such as Cassandra are true? Select all that apply.
options: Tables are usually designed around specific query patterns, often one table per query
Rows within a partition are stored sorted by clustering columns
Joins between tables are not supported by the query language
They store data column by column like analytics warehouses, which makes them ideal for large aggregations
Querying by a non-key column is as cheap as querying by the partition key
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: In Cassandra a partition key picks the node and clustering columns order rows within it; there are no joins, so you denormalize per query. 'Wide-column' doesn't mean columnar OLAP storage, and non-key filters need indexes or ALLOW FILTERING scans.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: 'Wide-column' databases like Cassandra are columnar analytics stores in the same category as ClickHouse or Redshift.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: Cassandra stores rows grouped by partition key, optimized for high write throughput and key-based reads. Columnar warehouses store each column contiguously for fast scans and aggregations. The names sound alike, but the designs differ.

dbms-nosql:0.prompt: A key-value store generally can't efficiently answer 'find all values where field X equals Y' unless you maintain your own index keys for that query.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:0.explanation: A pure key-value store only knows keys, so querying by value means a full scan unless you write extra index entries yourself (for example a set per city). That's why access patterns have to be designed up front.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: In MongoDB, a blog post has at most about 10 short comments, always displayed with the post and rarely queried on their own. How should comments be modelled?
options: Embed the comments as an array in the post document
Store comments in a separate collection, joined with $lookup on every read
One collection per post
Store each comment in Redis
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: A small, bounded set of children that is always read with the parent is the classic case for embedding: one read and atomic updates. $lookup on every read adds cost for no benefit at this size.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: What is the maximum size of a single BSON document in MongoDB?
options: 1 MB
4 MB
16 MB
64 MB
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: MongoDB documents are capped at 16 MB, which limits how much you can embed. Larger files belong in GridFS or object storage, and unbounded child lists belong in their own collection.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: A MongoDB user document embeds an `activity` array, and a new entry is pushed on every page view, forever. What is the problem?
options: Arrays can't be indexed
MongoDB doesn't allow $push on nested fields
Reads of the user become eventually consistent
The array grows without bound: documents bloat, every read loads it, and it can eventually hit the 16 MB limit
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Unbounded arrays are a well-known anti-pattern: document size and write cost keep growing, and the hard limit is eventually reached. Store activity in its own collection (perhaps bucketed by time) that references the user. Arrays can be indexed (multikey).

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: An orders collection stores customerId plus a copy of the customer's name and shipping address at order time (the extended reference pattern). Why?
options: The order page renders without a $lookup, and the copy records the address as it was when the order was placed
MongoDB forbids storing references alone
To avoid needing an index on customerId
So that changing a customer's address updates past orders automatically
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Duplicating a few stable or point-in-time fields saves a join on hot reads, and for orders the snapshot is actually correct historically. It does not update automatically; that's the trade-off, and here it's the desired behaviour.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: Every post document embeds the author's name and avatar URL. Authors change avatars occasionally, and some have 50,000 posts. What is the main cost of this design?
options: Reading a post needs a multi-document transaction
An avatar change must update every post by that author (a large fan-out write), or older posts show stale data
Posts can't be indexed by author
The 16 MB limit is reached quickly
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Duplication speeds up reads but turns one profile change into many writes, or forces you to accept staleness. It's fine when changes are rare and slight staleness is acceptable; otherwise reference the author and fetch or cache the profile.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: An order and its line items must be updated together atomically, and they are always read together. Why does embedding the line items in the order document help?
options: Embedded arrays are cached in RAM
MongoDB doesn't support transactions
Single-document writes are atomic, so order and items change together without a multi-document transaction
Embedding makes reads eventually consistent
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Any write to one document is atomic in MongoDB. Embedding data that must change together avoids the extra latency and complexity of a multi-document transaction. MongoDB does support those, so the second option is wrong.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: Each sensor in a MongoDB collection writes one reading per second. The team switches from one document per reading to one document per sensor per hour, holding an array of up to 3,600 readings (the bucket pattern). What do they gain?
options: Far fewer documents and index entries, with each hour's data read in one fetch
Automatic downsampling
Unlimited document size
Strong consistency across shards
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Bucketing groups many small readings into bounded documents, shrinking index size and document overhead and making time-range reads cheap. The bucket is bounded, so it stays far from 16 MB. MongoDB's native time-series collections apply a similar idea internally.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: Which signals suggest REFERENCING a child entity in its own collection rather than embedding it? Select all that apply.
options: The number of children can grow without bound
Children are often queried or updated on their own
The same child is shared by many parents
Children are always read together with the parent
There are a fixed, small number of children per parent
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: Unbounded growth, independent access and many-to-many sharing all favour separate documents. Always reading together and small fixed cardinality are the classic reasons to embed.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB's $lookup stage are true? Select all that apply.
options: It performs a left outer join, adding an array of matching documents
It is an aggregation pipeline stage
An index on the foreign collection's join field makes it much cheaper
Heavy $lookup use on hot read paths can be a sign the schema should embed or denormalize
It can be used inside a find() query filter
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: $lookup is an aggregation stage with left-outer-join semantics, and it benefits greatly from an index on foreignField. Frequent joins on hot paths often mean the data model fights the access pattern. It isn't available in find() filters.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: In MongoDB, an update that modifies several fields of one document is atomic even without a transaction.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: MongoDB guarantees atomicity at the single-document level, including embedded arrays and subdocuments. Transactions are only needed when several documents must change together.

dbms-nosql:1.prompt: Because MongoDB is schemaless, data modelling decisions like embed versus reference can easily be changed later without migrating existing documents.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:1.explanation: The schema is implicit, not absent. Moving from embedded to referenced data (or the reverse) means rewriting existing documents and changing every query that relies on the shape. Model around access patterns from the start.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: In MongoDB, a query is find({ status: 'active', age: { $gt: 30 } }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }). Following the Equality-Sort-Range rule, which compound index is best?
options: { age: 1, status: 1, createdAt: -1 }
{ createdAt: -1, age: 1, status: 1 }
{ status: 1, age: 1, createdAt: -1 }
{ status: 1, createdAt: -1, age: 1 }
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: Equality fields first narrow to one index range, the sort field next keeps results in index order (no in-memory sort), and range fields last. Putting age before createdAt would force a blocking sort.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: explain('executionStats') for a slow MongoDB query shows a winning plan stage of COLLSCAN. What does that mean?
options: The query used a covered index
No suitable index was used, so every document in the collection was scanned
The query ran across all shards
The result came from the plan cache
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: COLLSCAN means a full collection scan. Compare totalDocsExamined with nReturned and add an index matching the filter and sort. An index scan shows up as IXSCAN.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: A MongoDB collection has the compound index { a: 1, b: 1, c: 1 }. Which query can NOT use it efficiently as a prefix?
options: find({ a: 5 })
find({ a: 5, b: 2 })
find({ b: 2, c: 3 })
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: Compound indexes support queries on a leading prefix of their keys: a, then a+b, then a+b+c. A filter on b and c without a can't seek into the index, because entries are ordered by a first.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: An aggregation pipeline starts with $unwind on a large array, then $group, then $match on status. How can it be made much cheaper?
options: Move $match on status to the start so it can use an index and shrink the input before $unwind
Add $sort at the end
Replace $group with $project
Use allowDiskUse to speed it up
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: Filtering first lets the pipeline use an index and cuts the documents flowing into the expensive $unwind and $group stages. (The optimizer may move some stages itself, but writing $match early is the reliable rule.) allowDiskUse avoids memory errors; it doesn't speed things up.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: A developer runs a multi-document transaction against a local standalone mongod and gets an error. Why?
options: Transactions need MongoDB Atlas
Transactions only work on documents under 1 MB
Multi-document transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster; a single-node replica set is enough for development
Transactions must be enabled per collection
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: MongoDB transactions depend on replica set machinery (the oplog), so a standalone server rejects them. Running mongod as a one-member replica set is the usual dev setup. They work on self-hosted deployments too, not just Atlas.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: A MongoDB transaction fails with an error labelled TransientTransactionError. What should the application do?
options: Retry the entire transaction from the start
Retry only the commit
Treat the data as corrupted and alert
Ignore it, because the transaction committed
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: TransientTransactionError (for example a write conflict or a primary step-down) means the whole transaction can safely be re-run. UnknownTransactionCommitResult is the label that calls for retrying just the commit. The driver's withTransaction helper handles both.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: In MongoDB, a team tries to create the compound index { tags: 1, categories: 1 }, where both fields are arrays in the same documents. What happens?
options: The index builds normally as a multikey index
MongoDB indexes only the first element of each array
The index is created but ignored by the planner
MongoDB refuses to index documents where both fields are arrays ('cannot index parallel arrays')
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: A compound multikey index may have at most one array-valued field per document, because indexing the cross product of two arrays could explode. Inserting or indexing such documents fails. Use separate indexes, or restructure the data.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: A MongoDB query uses index { email: 1 } with projection { email: 1 }, but explain still shows a FETCH stage. What is the most likely reason?
options: The index is multikey
The projection includes _id by default, and _id isn't in the index, so documents must be fetched
The collection is sharded
email isn't unique
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: A covered query needs every projected field to be in the index. _id is returned unless excluded, so use { email: 1, _id: 0 } to get a pure IXSCAN. Uniqueness has nothing to do with coverage.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB TTL indexes are true? Select all that apply.
options: A TTL index is a single-field index on a date field with expireAfterSeconds
A background task removes expired documents about every 60 seconds, so documents can outlive their expiry briefly
Documents are deleted at the exact second they expire
A TTL index on a field holding a string like '2025-01-01' expires those documents normally
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: TTL deletion runs periodically, roughly every minute, and can lag under load, so don't rely on exact timing. The field must be a BSON Date (or an array of Dates); documents with strings or other types in it never expire.

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: Which statements about MongoDB multi-document transactions are true? Select all that apply.
options: Writes inside the transaction aren't visible outside it until it commits
Reads inside a transaction see a consistent snapshot
They add overhead, so modelling data to need only single-document atomicity is still preferred where practical
They work on a standalone mongod
They have no time limit by default
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: Transactions provide snapshot reads and all-or-nothing visibility, but they cost latency and resources, so MongoDB recommends schemas that mostly need single-document atomicity. They need a replica set or sharded cluster and abort after transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds (60s by default).

dbms-nosql:2.prompt: In MongoDB, the index { userId: 1, createdAt: -1 } can serve find({ userId: 7 }).sort({ createdAt: 1 }) without an in-memory sort.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:2.explanation: With equality on userId, the matching entries are ordered by createdAt descending, and MongoDB can walk the index backwards to get ascending order. Indexes can be traversed in either direction.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A game needs a real-time leaderboard with 'top 10 players' and 'what is my rank?' queries. Which Redis data structure fits?
options: List
Hash
Set
Sorted set (ZADD, ZREVRANGE, ZREVRANK)
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score, with O(log N) updates and fast range and rank queries. A plain set has no ordering, and a list would need a full re-sort on every score change.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: Why are concurrent INCR calls on the same Redis key safe without extra locking?
options: Redis takes a row lock per key
Redis runs each command atomically, executing commands one at a time on its main thread
INCR uses compare-and-swap retries in the client
Redis serializes keys to disk first
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: Commands execute one at a time on the main thread (I/O threads in Redis 6+ only handle network reads and writes), so each command is atomic. A client-side GET-then-SET would not be atomic, because other commands can run in between.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A fixed-window rate limiter runs INCR key and then, if the result is 1, sends EXPIRE key 60 as a separate command. What is the bug?
options: INCR isn't atomic
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero
If the process dies between INCR and EXPIRE, the key never expires and the user is blocked forever
The limit check should come before INCR
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: The two calls aren't atomic together. A crash or timeout after INCR leaves a counter with no TTL. Use a Lua script, a MULTI block, or SET key 0 EX 60 NX followed by INCR, so the TTL is always set.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A Redis lock is acquired with SET lock:job <random-token> NX PX 30000. Why release it with a Lua script that deletes the key only if its value equals your token, instead of a plain DEL?
options: DEL is slower than Lua
If your lock already expired and another client took it, a plain DEL would delete THEIR lock
Lua scripts make the lock survive restarts
DEL can't delete keys with a TTL
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: A long GC pause or slow job can outlive the TTL. Checking the token atomically ensures you only release a lock you still own. Even then, protect critical resources with fencing tokens, because expiry-based locks can't stop a paused holder from acting late.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: An admin script runs KEYS user:* on a production Redis with 50 million keys, and latency spikes for every client. Why, and what should it use?
options: KEYS is O(N) and blocks the single command thread until it finishes; use SCAN with MATCH to iterate incrementally
KEYS flushes the cache; use FLUSHDB instead
KEYS forces an AOF rewrite; use INFO instead
KEYS only works on replicas; use MONITOR
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: KEYS walks the whole keyspace in one blocking command, stalling everything else. SCAN returns a cursor and small batches, so other commands run in between, at the cost of possibly seeing keys more than once.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A Node service caches a hot product in Redis with a 60s TTL. Every 60s, latency spikes as thousands of requests miss at once and all query PostgreSQL. Which mitigation directly targets this?
options: Raise maxmemory
Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lru
Increase the TTL to 24 hours with no other change
Let only one request rebuild the value (a lock or single-flight) while others serve the stale value, and add TTL jitter or early refresh
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: This is a cache stampede. Coalescing rebuilds to one caller and refreshing before expiry stop the herd; jitter avoids synchronized expiries across keys. A longer TTL only makes the stampedes rarer and the data staler; memory settings don't help.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A notification service must not lose events if a consumer is down for a few minutes, and several workers should share the load. Why choose Redis Streams over Pub/Sub?
options: Pub/Sub can't deliver to more than one subscriber
Streams store messages and support consumer groups with acknowledgements (XACK) and pending-entry tracking; Pub/Sub drops messages for subscribers that aren't connected
Streams are faster than Pub/Sub for every workload
Pub/Sub messages expire after one second
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget: offline subscribers miss messages. Streams append to a log that consumers read from by ID, and consumer groups split work and track unacknowledged entries for redelivery. Pub/Sub does fan out to many subscribers.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: Which statements about Redis maxmemory-policy are true? Select all that apply.
options: Under noeviction, write commands that need more memory return errors once the limit is reached
volatile-* policies only consider keys that have a TTL
allkeys-lfu evicts the least frequently used keys across the whole keyspace
The default policy is allkeys-lru
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: The default is noeviction, which is a common surprise when Redis is used as a cache and writes start failing. Set allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache. volatile-* policies ignore keys without TTLs.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: Which statements about Redis persistence are true? Select all that apply.
options: With RDB snapshots only, a crash can lose all writes since the last snapshot
AOF with appendfsync everysec can lose about one second of writes on a crash
appendfsync always is the most durable AOF setting and the slowest
Taking an RDB snapshot has no cost regardless of dataset size
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: Durability depends on configuration: RDB is point-in-time, AOF everysec risks about one second, and always fsyncs every write. RDB snapshots fork the process, and copy-on-write can use a lot of extra memory and latency on large, write-heavy datasets.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: If one command inside a Redis MULTI/EXEC block fails at runtime (for example INCR on a string value), Redis rolls back the commands that already ran in that block.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: Redis transactions guarantee the commands run together without interleaving, but there is no rollback. A failing command returns an error and the others still apply. Only queue-time errors, such as syntax errors, abort the whole EXEC.

dbms-nosql:3.prompt: A Redis HyperLogLog can estimate the number of unique visitors using a small, fixed amount of memory per key, at the cost of a small approximation error.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:3.explanation: HyperLogLog uses at most about 12 KB per key, with a standard error around 0.81%, regardless of how many items are added. A Set gives exact counts, but its memory grows with every unique member.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: In DynamoDB (or Cassandra), what do the partition key and the sort key (clustering key) each do?
options: Both are hashed together to choose a node
The sort key chooses the node; the partition key orders items
The partition key decides which partition stores the item; the sort key orders items within that partition and enables range queries
The partition key must be unique per table; the sort key is optional metadata
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: The partition key is hashed to place data, and all items with that key live together, ordered by sort key. That makes 'all orders for customer X between dates A and B' a single efficient query. The partition key alone doesn't have to be unique when a sort key exists.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: In DynamoDB, what is the key difference between Query and Scan?
options: Query needs an equality condition on the partition key and reads only that partition; Scan reads the entire table
Scan is faster because it reads in parallel
Query can only return one item
They cost the same, but Scan supports filters
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: Query targets one partition key value (optionally a sort-key range), so its cost scales with the result. Scan reads every item and consumes capacity for all of them, even ones a filter later drops. Parallel scan only spreads that cost out.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: An events table in DynamoDB uses the current date ('2025-10-03') as its partition key. Under heavy write load, requests are throttled even though table capacity looks ample. Why, and what is a common fix?
options: Dates aren't valid partition keys; use numbers
Sort keys are missing; add one
DynamoDB limits tables to one write per second per day
All of today's writes hit one partition (a hot partition); add a random or computed suffix (write sharding) or use a higher-cardinality key
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: Throughput is limited per partition, so a low-cardinality key that funnels all writes to one value hits that partition's limit. Spreading writes across date#0 to date#N, and querying all suffixes when reading, distributes the load.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: A single-table DynamoDB design stores items like PK='CUSTOMER#123', SK='ORDER#2025-10-01#987'. How do you fetch all orders for customer 123, newest first?
options: Scan with a filter on PK
Query PK = 'CUSTOMER#123' AND begins_with(SK, 'ORDER#'), with ScanIndexForward = false
GetItem with PK only
Query SK = 'ORDER#' across all partitions
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: Putting the date in the sort key keeps orders sorted by date within the customer's partition, and ScanIndexForward=false reverses the order. GetItem needs the full primary key, and a key condition always requires partition-key equality.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: In DynamoDB, you need 'all orders with status = SHIPPED', but the table's partition key is customerId. What is the idiomatic approach?
options: Scan the table with a FilterExpression
Create a global secondary index (GSI) keyed on status (sharded if it's low cardinality), knowing that GSI reads are eventually consistent
Create a local secondary index on status after the table exists
Change the table's partition key in place
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: A GSI re-partitions the data by another attribute and can be added at any time; it's updated asynchronously. LSIs must be defined at table creation and keep the same partition key, and a table's primary key can't be changed in place. A low-cardinality key like status can itself become hot, so it may need sharding.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: In Cassandra, a query filters on a column that isn't part of the primary key, and the server refuses unless ALLOW FILTERING is added. What is the right fix for a frequent production query?
options: Add ALLOW FILTERING, which is just a performance hint
Raise the read timeout
Create another table, partitioned by that column, holding a denormalized copy of the data the query needs
Run the query at consistency level ALL
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: ALLOW FILTERING makes Cassandra scan many partitions and discard rows, which gets slower as data grows. The Cassandra way is query-first modelling: one table per access pattern, written together (for example with a logged batch). Consistency level doesn't change how much is scanned.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: A Cassandra table uses PRIMARY KEY (sensor_id, ts), and sensors report every second for years. Reads and compaction for old sensors get slower and slower. What is the problem, and the usual fix?
options: Partitions grow without bound; bucket the partition key by time, for example PRIMARY KEY ((sensor_id, day), ts)
ts should be the partition key
Cassandra can't store timestamps; use bigint
Increase the replication factor
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: Every reading for a sensor lands in one partition, which keeps growing. Huge partitions hurt reads, repairs and compaction. A compound partition key with a time bucket bounds partition size, and queries then hit one bucket per day. Making ts the partition key would scatter related rows and break range scans.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: Which statements about DynamoDB secondary indexes are true? Select all that apply.
options: A local secondary index (LSI) must be defined when the table is created
A global secondary index (GSI) supports strongly consistent reads
A GSI can use a different partition key from the base table
An LSI uses the same partition key as the base table, with a different sort key
A GSI can only be created when the table is created
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: LSIs share the base partition key, must be declared at table creation, and allow strongly consistent reads. GSIs choose any key, can be added or removed later, and only offer eventually consistent reads.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: A Cassandra keyspace has replication factor 3. Which statements about consistency levels are true? Select all that apply.
options: QUORUM writes plus QUORUM reads always overlap on at least one replica (2 + 2 > 3)
ONE writes plus ONE reads can return stale data
Writes at ALL fail if any one replica is down
ONE writes plus QUORUM reads guarantee reading the latest write
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: The R + W > N rule guarantees overlap: 2 + 2 = 4 > 3, but 1 + 2 = 3 isn't greater than 3, so a QUORUM read can miss the single replica that took the write. ALL needs every replica, so it trades availability for consistency.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: In DynamoDB, a FilterExpression on a Query reduces the read capacity consumed, because filtered-out items are never read.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: Filters are applied after items are read, so you pay for everything the key condition matched. To read less, push the condition into the key (a sort-key condition) or use an index.

dbms-nosql:4.prompt: A DynamoDB item can be at most 400 KB, so large blobs are usually stored in S3 with a pointer kept in the item.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:4.explanation: DynamoDB's item size limit is 400 KB, counting attribute names and values. Storing large payloads in object storage and keeping metadata plus the S3 key in DynamoDB is the standard pattern.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: A fintech ledger needs multi-row transactions, foreign keys, CHECK constraints and ad-hoc reporting by finance analysts. Which default choice is strongest?
options: A relational database such as PostgreSQL
Redis with AOF persistence
A graph database
DynamoDB with single-table design
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: Strong invariants, multi-entity atomicity and flexible SQL reporting are exactly where relational databases shine. DynamoDB can do transactions, but ad-hoc analytics and constraint enforcement would mostly be on you.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: A service has a few well-known access patterns (get by key, list by owner), needs predictable single-digit-millisecond latency at very large scale, and the team wants minimal operations work. What fits best?
options: A single PostgreSQL instance
A graph database
A managed key-value or document store such as DynamoDB, modelled around those access patterns
A columnar data warehouse
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: Known patterns plus massive scale plus low operations work is DynamoDB's sweet spot. A single PostgreSQL node may also work at moderate scale, but horizontal scaling and operations become your problem at very large scale. Warehouses aren't built for low-latency point reads.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: An early-stage startup's data is relational (users, teams, projects, permissions), and its query needs change weekly. Some entities have flexible custom fields. What's the pragmatic choice?
options: Cassandra, to be ready for scale
PostgreSQL, with JSONB columns for the flexible custom fields
One MongoDB collection per entity, joined with $lookup everywhere
Redis as the primary database
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: When access patterns are unknown and the data is relational, SQL's ad-hoc queries and constraints keep options open, and JSONB (indexable with GIN) covers the flexible parts. Cassandra needs query patterns fixed up front, which works against fast-changing requirements.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: A teammate argues for MongoDB 'because we won't need schema migrations'. What is the strongest counterpoint?
options: MongoDB requires DDL for every collection
MongoDB can't add fields to existing documents
Schemaless databases forbid indexes
The schema still exists in application code; changing document shapes still needs code that handles old and new shapes, or a backfill
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: 'Schemaless' means schema-on-read: the database won't stop shape drift, so the app must handle every version or you migrate data anyway. MongoDB can enforce structure with JSON Schema validation if you want it.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: A PostgreSQL products table has a JSONB attrs column, and queries like WHERE attrs @> '{"color": "red"}' are slow. What is the idiomatic fix?
options: Create a GIN index on attrs
Create a B-tree index on attrs
Move attrs to a separate MongoDB database
Cast attrs to text and use LIKE
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: GIN indexes support JSONB containment (@>) and key-existence operators. A B-tree on the whole JSONB value only helps equality on the entire document. This is a common reason PostgreSQL can cover document-style needs.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: In a design interview you're storing billions of chat messages, almost always read as 'latest N messages in conversation C', with very high write volume. Which data model fits best?
options: One normalized PostgreSQL table with an index on (conversation_id, created_at), on a single node forever
A graph database with one edge per message
A wide-column store partitioned by (conversation_id, time bucket) and clustered by message time descending
Redis lists as the system of record
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: The access pattern is fixed and partitionable, writes dominate, and data grows without bound, which suits wide-column stores (Discord famously used Cassandra, later ScyllaDB). Time buckets keep partitions bounded. A single-node PostgreSQL works at first but eventually hits write and storage limits.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: A request handler writes an order to PostgreSQL and then indexes it in Elasticsearch. Sometimes the second call fails, and search goes out of sync. What's the standard fix?
options: Write to Elasticsearch first
Wrap both calls in a database transaction
Retry the Elasticsearch call three times inline
Write an outbox row in the same PostgreSQL transaction (or use CDC from the WAL), and let an async worker update Elasticsearch
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: Two stores can't commit atomically, so dual writes always risk divergence. An outbox or CDC makes PostgreSQL the source of truth and propagates changes reliably and idempotently. A database transaction doesn't cover Elasticsearch, and inline retries still fail if the process crashes.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: Which questions belong in a sound SQL-versus-NoSQL decision? Select all that apply.
options: Are the access patterns known and stable, or still evolving?
Which invariants need multi-entity transactions?
What are the expected data size and write throughput, and do they exceed one node?
What does the team already know how to operate?
Which database is trending most this year?
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: Access patterns, consistency needs, scale and operational expertise drive the decision. Popularity says nothing about fit, and choosing on hype is a classic interview red flag.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: Which of these claims are MYTHS (false)? Select all that apply.
options: Relational databases can't scale horizontally
NoSQL databases never support transactions
Relational databases can't store or index JSON
Key-value stores generally need keys designed around access patterns up front
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: SQL can scale out (Citus, Vitess, CockroachDB, application sharding), MongoDB and DynamoDB support transactions, and PostgreSQL has indexable JSONB. The last statement is true: key-value stores really do require access-pattern-first design.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: PostgreSQL can serve many document-store needs through JSONB columns with GIN indexes, alongside its relational tables.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: JSONB stores parsed binary JSON with containment and path operators, and GIN indexes make those queries fast. Many teams use it to avoid running a separate document database.

dbms-nosql:5.prompt: Choosing a NoSQL database removes the need to think about data modelling, because you can store anything and query it any way later.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:5.explanation: Most NoSQL stores make you model for your queries up front (partition keys, embedding, denormalization). Querying in ways you didn't model for often means scans or rewrites. If anything, they need more upfront modelling than SQL.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: What does BASE stand for in the BASE versus ACID comparison?
options: Basically Atomic, Serializable, Eventually durable
Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent
Bounded Availability, Strong Errors
Batch Access, Snapshot Execution
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: BASE describes systems that prefer availability and let replicas converge over time, unlike ACID's immediate, strong guarantees.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: In ACID, what does Isolation mean?
options: Each transaction's changes are written to separate files
A committed transaction survives crashes
A transaction is all-or-nothing
Concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate states; ideally the result equals some serial order, depending on the isolation level
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: Isolation controls how concurrent transactions interact. SERIALIZABLE is the strongest level, and weaker levels allow specific anomalies. All-or-nothing is Atomicity, and surviving crashes is Durability.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: A user updates their display name, the page reloads, and the OLD name appears for a moment before the new one shows on a later refresh. In an eventually consistent system, what is the likely cause?
options: The write was lost
The read went to a replica that hadn't received the write yet; read-your-writes routing would fix it
The cache key collided with another user's
The transaction was rolled back
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: Eventual consistency allows replicas to lag. The write did land and later appears. Sending a user's reads to the leader (or to a replica known to be caught up) after their own writes gives read-your-writes consistency.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: How does the 'C' in ACID differ from the 'C' in CAP?
options: ACID C means preserving the database's invariants and constraints; CAP C means linearizability, where every read sees the latest write
They mean the same thing
ACID C is about replicas agreeing; CAP C is about foreign keys
ACID C applies only to NoSQL
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: ACID consistency means each transaction takes the database from one valid state to another (constraints hold). CAP consistency is about a single up-to-date view across replicas. Mixing them up is a common interview trap.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: In practice, what makes a committed PostgreSQL transaction durable even if the server loses power right after COMMIT returns?
options: The data pages were written to disk before COMMIT returned
The commit is retried after restart
The commit record was flushed (fsynced) to the WAL before COMMIT was acknowledged
Durability is only guaranteed after the next checkpoint
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: With synchronous_commit on, COMMIT waits for the WAL flush, and recovery replays the WAL to rebuild unwritten pages. Data pages are written lazily, and checkpoints only bound recovery time; they don't decide durability.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store, two replicas concurrently accept 'add item A' and 'add item B' to the same cart during a partition. The store resolves conflicts with last-write-wins (LWW) timestamps. What happens?
options: The cart ends up with both A and B
Both writes are rejected
The cart is locked until an operator intervenes
One of the additions is silently discarded, depending on whichever timestamp is later
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: LWW keeps one version and drops the other, so concurrent updates get lost (and clock skew can drop even 'later' writes). Merging, for example a set-union CRDT or application-level merge as in Amazon's Dynamo cart, keeps both items.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: A transfer transaction debits account A, and the process crashes before it credits account B. Which ACID property ensures A's balance is restored after recovery?
options: Atomicity
Isolation
Consistency
Durability
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: Atomicity means a transaction that didn't commit leaves no effects, so recovery rolls back the debit. Isolation is about concurrent transactions seeing each other's partial work, which isn't the issue here.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: Which techniques help an eventually consistent (BASE) system still give users a good experience? Select all that apply.
options: Read-your-writes, by routing a user's reads to the leader shortly after they write
Idempotent operations, so retries and redelivery are safe
CRDTs or merge functions that resolve concurrent updates without losing data
Assuming every replica in every region is up to date immediately after a write
Running two-phase commit across all replicas on every write
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: Session guarantees, idempotency and convergent data types make eventual consistency workable. Assuming instant consistency causes bugs, and global 2PC on every write abandons the availability that BASE was chosen for.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions
DynamoDB supports transactional writes across items (TransactWriteItems)
PostgreSQL's default isolation level is READ COMMITTED, not SERIALIZABLE
ACID databases always run transactions as SERIALIZABLE by default
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: The ACID-versus-BASE line has blurred: major NoSQL stores offer transactions. Meanwhile most relational databases default to weaker isolation (READ COMMITTED in PostgreSQL, REPEATABLE READ in MySQL InnoDB), so 'ACID' doesn't automatically mean serializable.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: Eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made, all replicas will eventually return the same value.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: That is the definition: convergence once writes stop. It says nothing about how long that takes, or what readers see in the meantime.

dbms-nosql:6.prompt: 'Soft state' in BASE means the data is only stored in memory and is lost on restart.
options: True
False
dbms-nosql:6.explanation: Soft state means the system's state may change over time even without new input, as replicas converge. It has nothing to do with being in memory; BASE systems such as Cassandra persist data durably.
